questions.question_text: A coin simulator shows tails $9$ times in $15$ trials. What is the observed probability of tails, as a fraction in simplest form?

options.why: Used the six non-tail trials as favourable instead of the nine tails.

questions.question_text: An outcome has expected probability $0.4$ and observed probability $0.35$. What is the absolute difference?

options.why: Added the two probabilities instead of finding their difference.
Ignored the hundredths place and subtracted three-tenths from four-tenths incorrectly.

questions.question_text: A simulator tests an expected probability of $0.5$. Which observed result is closer to expected?

options.why: Chose the smaller experiment without comparing its observed proportion with one-half.
Chose the result with a larger success count instead of the proportion closest to one-half.

questions.question_text: Why do large numbers of trials usually give an observed probability closer to the expected probability?

options.text: Random variation has less effect on the overall proportion.
The expected probability changes to match the observations.
options.why: Treated a fixed theoretical probability as if trial results could alter it.

options.text: Every outcome must occur equally often in a large experiment.
options.why: Confused closeness to expected proportions with equal frequencies for all outcomes.

questions.solution_text:
More trials reduce the effect of short random runs on the overall proportion.
The observed probability usually moves closer to the fixed expected probability.

questions.question_text: An expected probability is $\frac{1}{5}$. In $50$ trials, the outcome occurs $12$ times. How does the observed count compare with the expected count?

options.why: Reversed the direction after comparing the observed count 12 with expected count 10.
Compared the outcome count with the total trials instead of the expected count.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{expected count}=\frac{1}{5}\times50=10$
$12-10=2$
The observation is $2$ above expected.

questions.question_text: Two trials test an expected probability of $0.3$. Trial A observes $16$ of $40$ successes; trial B observes $87$ of $300$. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Trial B is closer: its difference is $0.01$.
Trial A is closer: its difference is $0.1$.
options.why: Correctly found Trial A's difference but failed to compare it with Trial B's smaller difference.

options.text: Both are equally close because they test the same probability.
options.why: Assumed a shared expected probability forces equal observed deviations.

questions.solution_text:
$A: \frac{16}{40}=0.4$, difference $0.1$.
$B: \frac{87}{300}=0.29$, difference $0.01$.
Trial B is closer.
